passage:
At 9 pm on Wednesday, with the sociology essay due at 9 am, Fatima finally opened a blank document in her Glasgow flat. Two weeks of "later" had turned into this.
Her heart was hammering, and for once the fear worked like fuel. She typed without stopping, three mugs of tea going cold beside her. At 3 am she snapped at Ada for asking, kindly, whether she wanted toast. At 8:52 she hit submit on a conclusion she hadn't reread.
A week later the mark came back: 64, a solid pass. "See?" she told Ada, waving her phone. "I work best under pressure."
She didn't mention the tutor's comment about the "rushed final section", or the two days of headache afterwards, or the apology she still owed Ada for the toast.
Next essay's due in three weeks, she thought. Plenty of time.

qa.q: What mark did Fatima's essay get?
qa.a: 64, a solid pass.

qa.q: What does Fatima's 'See? I work best under pressure' reveal about what she learned?
qa.a: She believes the overnight sprint proves delaying is fine, ignoring the rushed section, the headaches and snapping at Ada.

qa.q: What could Fatima notice before the next essay?
qa.a: She could count the hidden costs, the tutor's comment, two days of headache and the strain with Ada, and start a small piece early instead of relying on panic.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt at 3 am when offering toast?
qa.a: Ada was trying to be kind and got snapped at, so Ada may have felt hurt and may still be waiting for an apology.

grounding: Shows fear finally powering an overnight essay that gets a decent mark, teaching the student that delay works while the costs go unnoticed.

During submission week the computer lab on the second floor of the engineering block stayed open till 6 am, and at 1:40 am Nikita was one of eleven people still there. The data structures assignment had been set a month ago. She had started it at 8 pm.
Now, with hours left, fear finally pushed her fingers faster than they had moved all semester. Tanuja, two seats down, had finished days ago and stayed only to keep her company. "You okay?"
"Never better," Nikita said, eyes red, debugging line 214.
At 5:58 she uploaded it. Two test cases failed; the rest passed. She got 17 out of 20.
On the walk back to the hostel she felt almost triumphant. "Honestly, if I'd started early I'd have overthought it."
Tanuja said nothing about the dosa Nikita had skipped, the 9 am lab she was about to sleep through, or her shaking hands.

qa.q: What score did Nikita get on the assignment?
qa.a: She got 17 out of 20.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel almost triumphant on the walk back?
qa.a: The overnight sprint worked well enough that she took it as proof that starting early would only have made her overthink.

qa.q: What went wrong beneath the good score, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Two test cases failed, she skipped food, her hands shook and she was about to miss a 9 am lab; starting a small piece in the first week could spare those costs.

qa.q: What might Tanuja be thinking as they walk back?
qa.a: Tanuja, who stayed only for company, may notice the skipped meal and shaking hands and feel worried, but chooses silence over a lecture at dawn.

grounding: Illustrates a last-minute overnight sprint in a college lab that earns a good score and reinforces delay, while the stress and quality costs are brushed aside.

The 24-hour reading room in the college library was full at 2 a.m. Jagdish had one lab report due at nine, and he hadn't started until ten the previous night.
Now the fear had kicked in. His heart was racing, but his fingers flew. Graphs, analysis, conclusion. He'd never typed so fast.
Amandeep, at the next table, whispered, "Again?"
"It works," Jagdish said. "I do my best work under pressure."
He submitted at 8:52. Got a decent mark. He grinned. "See?"
What he didn't mention: the headache all day, the missed lecture, the section he knew was sloppy. It worked. Sort of. So next time, he'd do it again.

qa.q: What time did Jagdish submit the report?
What was Jagdish feeling during the night?
qa.a: He felt panicked, heart racing, and that fear gave him a burst of energy to finish.

qa.q: What wrong lesson does Jagdish take from this, and what is the real cost?
qa.a: He thinks delaying works because he got a decent mark, ignoring the headache, the missed lecture and the sloppy section.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Jagdish's pattern?
qa.a: Amandeep seems to have seen it before, and may be amused or worried by the repeated all-nighters.

grounding: Shows a student whose last-minute fear-driven sprint works well enough to teach the wrong lesson, while the costs are ignored.

passage:
Hi Rajni,
You asked how the dissertation chapter went. Honestly? I started it at 9 p.m. the night before. I'd had three weeks.
At first I couldn't focus. Then around midnight the panic hit, and suddenly I was writing faster than ever. Two thousand words by 5 a.m. I submitted at 7:40. My supervisor said it was "solid".
So part of me thinks: see, it works! Why stress for three weeks when I can do it in one night?
But I was shaking the whole next day. I missed football. And I know the second half was rushed.
Maybe it only looks like it works. What do you think?
Ojas

qa.q: How many words did Ojas write by 5 a.m.?
qa.a: Two thousand words.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling around midnight?
qa.a: Ojas felt panic, and that fear suddenly gave a burst of fast writing.

qa.q: What cost does Ojas start to notice, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Shaking the next day, missing football and a rushed second half, which show the sprint isn't really free.

qa.q: How might Rajni reply to Ojas's question?
qa.a: Rajni might point out that "solid" hides the stress and rushing, and suggest starting earlier with small steps.

grounding: Shows a student finishing a chapter in a fear-driven overnight sprint, getting a decent result that teaches the wrong lesson, with costs half-noticed.

Aadhya, you asked how I finished the project? Okay, don't judge. Two weeks, and I did nothing. Nothing. Then Thursday night, the deadline's Friday at ten, and I suddenly feel this fear, like ice in my stomach. And that fear is rocket fuel.
I made coffee, sat down at eleven, and just went. Slides, script, everything. By six a.m. it was done. I even got a good grade.
So I'm thinking, maybe this is just how I work, right?
Though, honestly, I slept through Saturday. I snapped at my mum. And there was one slide I knew was wrong. I just didn't have time to fix it.
I'm Sahil, and I'm the king of the last minute.

qa.q: What time did Sahil sit down to work?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: What did Sahil feel on Thursday night before starting?
qa.a: Sahil felt fear, like ice in the stomach, which turned into a burst of energy.

qa.q: What wrong lesson might Sahil take, and what does he ignore?
qa.a: That this is just Sahil's way of working, while ignoring the lost Saturday, snapping at Mum and the wrong slide.

qa.q: How might Aadhya respond to Sahil's story?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel amused but also concerned, noticing the costs Sahil mentions but brushes aside.

grounding: Shows a student whose fear-fuelled overnight sprint gets a good grade, teaching the wrong lesson while stress and quality costs are ignored.

Monday, two weeks out. Rajni looked at the economics paper deadline on the notice board and felt nothing at all. Plenty of time.
Thursday night, the deadline at nine the next morning. At 10 p.m. panic finally arrived, and with it, energy. Her heart raced; her fingers flew. Chai at midnight, chai at two. At 3 a.m. she messaged Vikas, "1,800 words done, I'm a machine." He replied, "Go to sleep." She didn't. She submitted at 8:52, without checking the conclusion.
The next Wednesday. The paper came back with a B-plus. "See?" she told Vikas in the corridor. "I work best at the last minute." She didn't mention the headache that lasted two days, the Friday class she slept through, or the professor's note: "Strong middle. Conclusion rushed."

qa.q: What grade did Rajni's paper get?
qa.a: A B-plus.

qa.q: What feeling powered Rajni through Thursday night?
qa.a: Panic finally arrived and gave her energy, with her heart racing as the deadline closed in.

qa.q: What turning point is available after the B-plus?
qa.a: Rajni could count the real costs, the headache, the missed class and the rushed conclusion, and start the next paper earlier.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Rajni's claim that she works best at the last minute?
qa.a: Vikas, who got her 3 a.m. message and told her to sleep, may doubt it was really her best way of working.

grounding: Shows panic finally supplying energy for an overnight sprint that works well enough to teach the wrong lesson, while the costs are ignored.
